# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Radiation environment
excerpt: Mars lacks a global magnetic field and has a thin atmosphere (~16–20 g/cm² column vs. ~1,000 g/cm² on Earth). Curiosity RAD measured ≈ 0.64 ± 0.12 mSv/day on the surface at Gale (Hassler et al. 2014) and ≈ 1.8 mSv/day during cruise. A ~860-day reference mission (cruise + 500 days on the surface) accumulates roughly 1 Sv in total — comparable to or above career limits under older NASA standards. Solar particle events add acute risk; shielding with regolith, water or subsurface habitats reduces dose. Lower-elevation sites have slightly more atmospheric shielding. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: Quick explainer on radiation environment?
Mars lacks a global magnetic field and has a thin atmosphere (~16–20 g/cm² column vs. ~1,000 g/cm² on Earth). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: neuronexus_project.md / What NeuroNexus does
excerpt: Synchronised 2D Mars map, USGS scientific map (SIM 3292 geology) and interactive 3D Mars (ArcGIS SceneView, Mars 2000 coordinates). 2,052 USGS/IAU named features are searchable, and any coordinate can be selected. Site context: NASA MOLA terrain (elevation, slope, roughness, with AT SITE / MIN / MEAN / MAX over a selectable window); historical NASA THEMIS thermal evidence; the NASA Ames MY34 dust scenario (opacity chart over all 668 sols, dust-top height, global dust map, sol scrubber); site science and habitability context; rover imagery. Routes: manual multi-waypoint routes; the AI Route Designer (deterministic multi-objective candidates over MOLA terrain: EVA, terrain, science and operational objectives); saved routes with along-track MIN / MEAN / MAX statistics, shown in 2D and 3D; side-by-side comparison with best/worst marking and elevation profiles; per-route and combined USGS snapshots; JSON/CSV exports. Mission awareness: Crewed Mars console (mission profile, EVA, life support, resources), NASA/JPL near-Mars small-body close-approach tracking, and the NASA Mars reference feed. Mars Intelligence: a Gemini-powered assistant that answers from application tools, a curated Mars knowledge base and project documentation, with optional Google Search grounding. It never generates route geometry and never alters deterministic numbers. [KNOWLEDGE:neuronexus_project.md]

Synchronised 2D Mars map, USGS scientific map (SIM 3292 geology) and interactive 3D Mars (ArcGIS SceneView, Mars 2000 coordinates). 2,052 USGS/IAU named features are searchable, and any coordinate can be selected. Site context: NASA MOLA terrain (elevation, slope, roughness, with AT SITE / MIN / MEAN / MAX over a selectable window); historical NASA THEMIS thermal evidence; the NASA Ames MY34 dust scenario (opacity chart over all 668 sols, dust-top height, global dust map, sol scrubber); site science and habitability context; rover imagery. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / In-situ resource utilisation (ISRU)
excerpt: Oxygen from atmospheric CO₂ by solid-oxide electrolysis. Perseverance MOXIE produced 122 g O₂ in total, up to ~12 g/h at ~98% purity. Water from ground ice (mid and high latitudes) or hydrated minerals. Water is the key resource for life support, radiation shielding and propellant. Methane/oxygen propellant via the Sabatier reaction (CO₂ + H₂ → CH₄ + H₂O), the basis of many return-vehicle concepts. Regolith for shielding, construction (sintering, 3D printing) and agriculture after perchlorate removal. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Seasons and solar longitude (Ls)
excerpt: Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Because of the eccentric orbit, perihelion falls near Ls 251° (southern late spring/summer). Southern summers are shorter and hotter; northern summers longer and cooler. The dusty season is roughly Ls 180°–360° (southern spring/summer); regional storms are common then and planet-encircling (global) dust storms occur in some years. Mars Years (MY) follow the Clancy et al. (2000) convention: MY 1 began on 11 April 1955 (Ls 0). MY 34 began 5 May 2017; MY 35 began 23 March 2019; MY 37 began 26 December 2022; MY 38 began 12 November 2024. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

Spirit (MER-A, NASA): landed 4 January 2004 in Gusev crater; found evidence of hydrothermal activity (silica-rich deposits at Home Plate). Became stuck in 2009; last communication 22 March 2010. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / EVA and traverse planning concepts used in NeuroNexus
excerpt: EVA time is estimated from distance divided by pace, plus an ascent allowance (metres climbed per hour). In NeuroNexus the defaults are 2.5 km/h and 600 m/h, and both are user adjustable. Slope: Apollo-era and analog studies suggest walking becomes markedly harder above ~15° and rovers are commonly limited to ~15–30° depending on design. Roughness: here this means local elevation variability (m) in a 3×3 MOLA neighbourhood, a coarse (~460 m pixel) proxy. It does not resolve boulders; HiRISE-scale data is needed for that. Safe Haven: in NeuroNexus, a user-designated retreat point (habitat, cache, rover). Routes report the maximum distance from the nearest Safe Haven. This is a planning aid only; nothing in NeuroNexus certifies a location as safe. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

excerpt: Polar caps: north residual cap is mostly water ice (~1,000 km across, layered deposits up to ~3 km thick); the south residual cap has a thin CO₂ ice veneer over water ice. Ground ice is widespread poleward of ~±40–50° latitude; Phoenix (2008, 68° N) exposed water ice a few centimetres below the surface. Fresh impact craters and exposed scarps (HiRISE) reveal relatively pure ice at mid-latitudes, important for human ISRU. Ancient water evidence: valley networks, deltas (Jezero, Eberswalde), lake sediments (Gale), hydrated minerals (clays, sulfates, carbonates), hematite concretions (Meridiani). Recurring slope lineae (RSL) were once proposed as brines but are now widely interpreted as granular flows; treat claims of present-day liquid water with caution. Perchlorate salts (found by Phoenix, confirmed by Curiosity) are common in the soil; they are toxic to humans and lower the freezing point of brines. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / EVA and traverse planning concepts used in NeuroNexus
excerpt: EVA time is estimated from distance divided by pace, plus an ascent allowance (metres climbed per hour). In NeuroNexus the defaults are 2.5 km/h and 600 m/h, and both are user adjustable. Slope: Apollo-era and analog studies suggest walking becomes markedly harder above ~15° and rovers are commonly limited to ~15–30° depending on design. Roughness: here this means local elevation variability (m) in a 3×3 MOLA neighbourhood, a coarse (~460 m pixel) proxy. It does not resolve boulders; HiRISE-scale data is needed for that. Safe Haven: in NeuroNexus, a user-designated retreat point (habitat, cache, rover). Routes report the maximum distance from the nearest Safe Haven. This is a planning aid only; nothing in NeuroNexus certifies a location as safe. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

QUESTION: Background on eva and traverse planning concepts used in neuronexus, please.

EVA time is estimated from distance divided by pace, plus an ascent allowance (meters climbed per hour). In NeuroNexus the defaults are 2.5 km/h and 600 m/h, and both are user adjustable. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Human exploration: architecture and constraints
excerpt: Transit: Hohmann-like transfers take ~6–9 months each way. Departure windows open every ~26 months. A conjunction-class mission lasts ~2.5–3 years in total with ~500 days on the surface. An opposition-class mission is shorter overall (~1.5–2 years) but has only ~30–60 days on the surface and higher Δv. Entry, descent and landing for human-class payloads (tens of tonnes) is unsolved at scale. Supersonic retropropulsion and inflatable decelerators (e.g. LOFTID) are being matured. Communications delay is 3–22 min one way, and there is a ~2-week blackout at solar conjunction. Crews must operate autonomously; NeuroNexus' deterministic, offline-capable planning tools are designed with this in mind. Radiation: the surface dose is ~0.64 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD). Shielding options are regolith berms, water walls, lava tubes and subsurface habitats; storm shelters are needed for solar particle events. Dust: fine, abrasive and electrostatically charged; contains perchlorates (a thyroid toxin); degrades seals, solar arrays and thermal radiators. Suitports, dust-tolerant mechanisms and airlock cleaning are required. Temperature: night lows below −80 °C are routine at mid-latitudes, so habitats, rovers and suits need active thermal control. Gravity: 0.38 g. Long-term health effects of partial gravity are unknown; crews arrive deconditioned after months in microgravity. excerpt: Composition (Curiosity SAM, Gale crater): ≈ 95% CO₂, ≈ 2.6–2.8% N₂, ≈ 1.9–2.0% Ar, ≈ 0.16–0.17% O₂, ≈ 0.06% CO, plus trace H₂O and other species. Exact fractions vary seasonally. Mean surface pressure ≈ 600 Pa (≈ 0.6% of Earth's). It varies by ~25–30% over the year as CO₂ freezes onto and sublimes from the seasonal polar caps, and strongly with elevation: ~1,100+ Pa in Hellas, well under 100 Pa at the top of Olympus Mons. 610 Pa is the reference "mean" pressure used to normalise dust optical depths (Montabone et al.). Temperatures: global mean ≈ 210 K (−63 °C). Surface extremes span roughly −125 °C (polar night, CO₂ frost point ≈ 148 K at 600 Pa) to about +20 °C (equatorial summer afternoons, dark surfaces). The thin air holds little heat, so diurnal swings of 70–100 K are normal. Liquid water is unstable at the surface almost everywhere: pressure is near the triple point of water (611.657 Pa). excerpt: Pre-Noachian (> ~4.1 Ga): crust formation, dichotomy, early magnetic field. excerpt: Ancient astronomers tracked Mars' retrograde loops. Its red colour linked it to war gods (Nergal, Ares, Mars). Galileo first observed Mars telescopically in 1610. Christiaan Huygens drew the first surface feature, Syrtis Major, in 1659 and estimated the rotation period. Giovanni Cassini refined the period and noted the polar caps (1666). William Herschel measured the axial tilt and noted seasonal polar cap changes (1780s). 1877 opposition: Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped "canali" (channels), mistranslated as "canals". Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos. Percival Lowell (1890s–1910s) popularised the idea of artificial canals. Better telescopes (Antoniadi, 1909) and later Mariner 4 (1965) showed the canals were optical illusions. Spacecraft era: see the missions reference. Key paradigm shifts: Mariner 4 showed a Moon-like cratered planet. Mariner 9 revealed volcanoes, canyons and ancient channels. Viking searched for life. # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Dust, dust storms and dust devils
excerpt: Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. Planet-encircling dust storms occurred in 1971 (Mariner 9 arrival), 1977 (two, Viking era), 2001, 2007 and 2018 (MY 34). The 2018 storm began near Ls ≈ 185° and ended the Opportunity rover's mission (power loss, last contact 10 June 2018). Dust lowers daytime surface temperature, raises atmospheric temperature, cuts solar-array output and increases electrostatic and abrasion hazards for hardware and EVA suits. Dust devils are common in spring and summer; they cleaned Spirit's and Opportunity's solar arrays several times. The Montabone et al. (2015) climatology reconstructs daily gridded column dust optical depth for MY 24 onward from orbiter (TES, THEMIS, MCS) retrievals. The NASA Ames Mars GCM V3.2 distributes it as DustScenario_MYxx.nc files (3° × 3° bins, daily) — this is the source of the NeuroNexus dust panel (variable `tau`, with `zmax` the dust-top altitude in km of the modified Conrath vertical profile). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Atmosphere
excerpt: Composition (Curiosity SAM, Gale crater): ≈ 95% CO₂, ≈ 2.6–2.8% N₂, ≈ 1.9–2.0% Ar, ≈ 0.16–0.17% O₂, ≈ 0.06% CO, plus trace H₂O and other species. Exact fractions vary seasonally. Mean surface pressure ≈ 600 Pa (≈ 0.6% of Earth's). It varies by ~25–30% over the year as CO₂ freezes onto and sublimes from the seasonal polar caps, and strongly with elevation: ~1,100+ Pa in Hellas, well under 100 Pa at the top of Olympus Mons. 610 Pa is the reference "mean" pressure used to normalise dust optical depths (Montabone et al.). Temperatures: global mean ≈ 210 K (−63 °C). Surface extremes span roughly −125 °C (polar night, CO₂ frost point ≈ 148 K at 600 Pa) to about +20 °C (equatorial summer afternoons, dark surfaces). The thin air holds little heat, so diurnal swings of 70–100 K are normal. Liquid water is unstable at the surface almost everywhere: pressure is near the triple point of water (611.657 Pa). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Selecting a human landing site / exploration zone
excerpt: NASA's First Landing Site/Exploration Zone Workshop (2015) defined an Exploration Zone (EZ) as ~100 km in radius around a landing site. Criteria: Engineering: latitude within ~±50° for solar power and thermal reasons; low elevation (below about +2 km MOLA) so the atmosphere helps braking; low slopes and rock abundance at the landing ellipse; load-bearing surfaces. Resources: accessible water ice or hydrated minerals; potential construction materials. Science: Regions of Interest (ROIs) with diverse, ancient geology (astrobiology, climate, volcanism) within traverse range. Operations: safe traverses for pressurised rovers and EVA. Walkback distance to the habitat drives EVA planning. NeuroNexus shows candidate Potential Exploration Zones in the 3D view. These are planning context, not certified sites. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Dust, dust storms and dust devils
excerpt: Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. Planet-encircling dust storms occurred in 1971 (Mariner 9 arrival), 1977 (two, Viking era), 2001, 2007 and 2018 (MY 34). The 2018 storm began near Ls ≈ 185° and ended the Opportunity rover's mission (power loss, last contact 10 June 2018). Dust lowers daytime surface temperature, raises atmospheric temperature, cuts solar-array output and increases electrostatic and abrasion hazards for hardware and EVA suits. Dust devils are common in spring and summer; they cleaned Spirit's and Opportunity's solar arrays several times. The Montabone et al. (2015) climatology reconstructs daily gridded column dust optical depth for MY 24 onward from orbiter (TES, THEMIS, MCS) retrievals. The NASA Ames Mars GCM V3.2 distributes it as DustScenario_MYxx.nc files (3° × 3° bins, daily) — this is the source of the NeuroNexus dust panel (variable `tau`, with `zmax` the dust-top altitude in km of the modified Conrath vertical profile). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: Background on dust, dust storms and dust devils, please.

Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Human exploration: architecture and constraints
excerpt: Transit: Hohmann-like transfers take ~6–9 months each way. Departure windows open every ~26 months. A conjunction-class mission lasts ~2.5–3 years in total with ~500 days on the surface. An opposition-class mission is shorter overall (~1.5–2 years) but has only ~30–60 days on the surface and higher Δv. Entry, descent and landing for human-class payloads (tens of tonnes) is unsolved at scale. Supersonic retropropulsion and inflatable decelerators (e.g. LOFTID) are being matured. Communications delay is 3–22 min one way, and there is a ~2-week blackout at solar conjunction. Crews must operate autonomously; NeuroNexus' deterministic, offline-capable planning tools are designed with this in mind. Radiation: the surface dose is ~0.64 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD). Shielding options are regolith berms, water walls, lava tubes and subsurface habitats; storm shelters are needed for solar particle events. Dust: fine, abrasive and electrostatically charged; contains perchlorates (a thyroid toxin); degrades seals, solar arrays and thermal radiators. Suitports, dust-tolerant mechanisms and airlock cleaning are required. Temperature: night lows below −80 °C are routine at mid-latitudes, so habitats, rovers and suits need active thermal control. Gravity: 0.38 g. Long-term health effects of partial gravity are unknown; crews arrive deconditioned after months in microgravity. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Observation history
excerpt: Ancient astronomers tracked Mars' retrograde loops. Its red colour linked it to war gods (Nergal, Ares, Mars). Galileo first observed Mars telescopically in 1610. Christiaan Huygens drew the first surface feature, Syrtis Major, in 1659 and estimated the rotation period. Giovanni Cassini refined the period and noted the polar caps (1666). William Herschel measured the axial tilt and noted seasonal polar cap changes (1780s). 1877 opposition: Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped "canali" (channels), mistranslated as "canals". Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos. Percival Lowell (1890s–1910s) popularised the idea of artificial canals. Better telescopes (Antoniadi, 1909) and later Mariner 4 (1965) showed the canals were optical illusions. Spacecraft era: see the missions reference. Key paradigm shifts: Mariner 4 showed a Moon-like cratered planet. Mariner 9 revealed volcanoes, canyons and ancient channels. Viking searched for life. MGS, Odyssey, MRO and the rovers established a wet, potentially habitable ancient Mars. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_missions.md / 2012–2020
excerpt: Curiosity / Mars Science Laboratory (NASA): landed 6 August 2012 (UTC) in Gale crater using the Sky Crane. It is a nuclear-powered (MMRTG) rover climbing Aeolis Mons (Mount Sharp). Its RAD instrument measured the surface radiation dose. MAVEN (NASA): orbit 21 September 2014; it studies upper-atmosphere loss to space, and showed that solar-wind stripping removed much of the early atmosphere. Verify its current status. Mars Orbiter Mission / Mangalyaan (ISRO, India): orbit 24 September 2014, India's first interplanetary mission, successful on its first attempt. Contact was lost in 2022. ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (ESA): orbit October 2016; studies trace gases (methane upper limits) and mapped hydrogen; also a relay. Its Schiaparelli demonstrator lander crashed on 19 October 2016. InSight (NASA): landed 26 November 2018 in Elysium Planitia. Its SEIS seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and constrained the size of Mars' crust, mantle and liquid core. The mission ended in December 2022 when dust starved its solar arrays. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_missions.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Water and ice
excerpt: Polar caps: north residual cap is mostly water ice (~1,000 km across, layered deposits up to ~3 km thick); the south residual cap has a thin CO₂ ice veneer over water ice. Ground ice is widespread poleward of ~±40–50° latitude; Phoenix (2008, 68° N) exposed water ice a few centimetres below the surface. Fresh impact craters and exposed scarps (HiRISE) reveal relatively pure ice at mid-latitudes, important for human ISRU. Ancient water evidence: valley networks, deltas (Jezero, Eberswalde), lake sediments (Gale), hydrated minerals (clays, sulfates, carbonates), hematite concretions (Meridiani). Recurring slope lineae (RSL) were once proposed as brines but are now widely interpreted as granular flows; treat claims of present-day liquid water with caution. Perchlorate salts (found by Phoenix, confirmed by Curiosity) are common in the soil; they are toxic to humans and lower the freezing point of brines. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

InSight (NASA): landed 26 November 2018 in Elysium Planitia. Its SEIS seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and constrained the size of Mars' crust, mantle and liquid core. The mission ended in December 2022 when dust starved its solar arrays. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_missions.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / EVA and traverse planning concepts used in NeuroNexus
excerpt: EVA time is estimated from distance divided by pace, plus an ascent allowance (metres climbed per hour). In NeuroNexus the defaults are 2.5 km/h and 600 m/h, and both are user adjustable. Slope: Apollo-era and analog studies suggest walking becomes markedly harder above ~15° and rovers are commonly limited to ~15–30° depending on design. Roughness: here this means local elevation variability (m) in a 3×3 MOLA neighbourhood, a coarse (~460 m pixel) proxy. It does not resolve boulders; HiRISE-scale data is needed for that. Safe Haven: in NeuroNexus, a user-designated retreat point (habitat, cache, rover). Routes report the maximum distance from the nearest Safe Haven. This is a planning aid only; nothing in NeuroNexus certifies a location as safe. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

QUESTION: What should the crew know about eva and traverse planning concepts used in neuronexus?

EVA time is estimated from distance divided by pace, plus an ascent allowance (meters climbed per hour). In NeuroNexus the defaults are 2.5 km/h and 600 m/h, and both are user adjustable. Slope: Apollo-era and analog studies suggest walking becomes markedly harder above ~15° and rovers are commonly limited to ~15–30° depending on design. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Bulk properties
excerpt: Mean radius 3,389.5 km (equatorial 3,396.2 km, polar 3,376.2 km). About 53% of Earth's radius. Mass 6.417 × 10^23 kg (≈ 10.7% of Earth). Mean density 3,933 kg/m³. Surface gravity 3.71–3.72 m/s² (≈ 0.38 g). A 100 kg astronaut-plus-suit system weighs as 38 kg would on Earth. Escape velocity 5.03 km/s. Low Mars orbit velocity ≈ 3.4–3.6 km/s. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Mars time keeping
excerpt: A sol is 24 h 39 m 35 s. Mission teams count sols from landing (Curiosity sol 0 = 6 August 2012). Local Mean Solar Time (LMST) and Local True Solar Time (LTST) are used for operations. "Mars time" shifts ~40 minutes later each Earth day, which is hard on ground crews. Coordinated Mars Time (MTC) is the mean solar time at the prime meridian (Airy-0 crater). Mars Year numbering (Clancy et al. 2000): MY 1 began 11 April 1955. The NeuroNexus dust scenario covers MY 34 (2017–2019), which includes the 2018 global dust storm. Longitude conventions: modern NASA and USGS products use planetocentric latitude and east-positive longitude 0–360° (NeuroNexus uses this). Older maps used planetographic latitude and west longitude. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Dust, dust storms and dust devils
excerpt: Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. Planet-encircling dust storms occurred in 1971 (Mariner 9 arrival), 1977 (two, Viking era), 2001, 2007 and 2018 (MY 34). The 2018 storm began near Ls ≈ 185° and ended the Opportunity rover's mission (power loss, last contact 10 June 2018). Dust lowers daytime surface temperature, raises atmospheric temperature, cuts solar-array output and increases electrostatic and abrasion hazards for hardware and EVA suits. Dust devils are common in spring and summer; they cleaned Spirit's and Opportunity's solar arrays several times. The Montabone et al. (2015) climatology reconstructs daily gridded column dust optical depth for MY 24 onward from orbiter (TES, THEMIS, MCS) retrievals. The NASA Ames Mars GCM V3.2 distributes it as DustScenario_MYxx.nc files (3° × 3° bins, daily) — this is the source of the NeuroNexus dust panel (variable `tau`, with `zmax` the dust-top altitude in km of the modified Conrath vertical profile). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: Explain dust, dust storms and dust devils briefly.

Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. Planet-encircling dust storms occurred in 1971 (Mariner 9 arrival), 1977 (two, Viking era), 2001, 2007 and 2018 (MY 34). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_missions.md / 2012–2020
excerpt: Curiosity / Mars Science Laboratory (NASA): landed 6 August 2012 (UTC) in Gale crater using the Sky Crane. It is a nuclear-powered (MMRTG) rover climbing Aeolis Mons (Mount Sharp). It established that Gale once held a long-lived, habitable freshwater lake (Yellowknife Bay, 2013). It detected complex organic molecules (2018) and seasonal methane variations. Its RAD instrument measured the surface radiation dose. MAVEN (NASA): orbit 21 September 2014; it studies upper-atmosphere loss to space, and showed that solar-wind stripping removed much of the early atmosphere. Verify its current status. Mars Orbiter Mission / Mangalyaan (ISRO, India): orbit 24 September 2014, India's first interplanetary mission, successful on its first attempt. Contact was lost in 2022. ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (ESA): orbit October 2016; studies trace gases (methane upper limits) and mapped hydrogen; also a relay. Its Schiaparelli demonstrator lander crashed on 19 October 2016. InSight (NASA): landed 26 November 2018 in Elysium Planitia. Its SEIS seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and constrained the size of Mars' crust, mantle and liquid core. The mission ended in December 2022 when dust starved its solar arrays. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_missions.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Mars time keeping
excerpt: A sol is 24 h 39 m 35 s. Mission teams count sols from landing (Curiosity sol 0 = 6 August 2012). Local Mean Solar Time (LMST) and Local True Solar Time (LTST) are used for operations. "Mars time" shifts ~40 minutes later each Earth day, which is hard on ground crews. Coordinated Mars Time (MTC) is the mean solar time at the prime meridian (Airy-0 crater). Mars Year numbering (Clancy et al. 2000): MY 1 began 11 April 1955. The NeuroNexus dust scenario covers MY 34 (2017–2019), which includes the 2018 global dust storm. Longitude conventions: modern NASA and USGS products use planetocentric latitude and east-positive longitude 0–360° (NeuroNexus uses this). Older maps used planetographic latitude and west longitude. # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Atmosphere
excerpt: Composition (Curiosity SAM, Gale crater): ≈ 95% CO₂, ≈ 2.6–2.8% N₂, ≈ 1.9–2.0% Ar, ≈ 0.16–0.17% O₂, ≈ 0.06% CO, plus trace H₂O and other species. Exact fractions vary seasonally. Mean surface pressure ≈ 600 Pa (≈ 0.6% of Earth's). It varies by ~25–30% over the year as CO₂ freezes onto and sublimes from the seasonal polar caps, and strongly with elevation: ~1,100+ Pa in Hellas, well under 100 Pa at the top of Olympus Mons. 610 Pa is the reference "mean" pressure used to normalise dust optical depths (Montabone et al.). Temperatures: global mean ≈ 210 K (−63 °C). Surface extremes span roughly −125 °C (polar night, CO₂ frost point ≈ 148 K at 600 Pa) to about +20 °C (equatorial summer afternoons, dark surfaces). The thin air holds little heat, so diurnal swings of 70–100 K are normal. Liquid water is unstable at the surface almost everywhere: pressure is near the triple point of water (611.657 Pa). excerpt: Pre-Noachian (> ~4.1 Ga): crust formation, dichotomy, early magnetic field. Noachian (~4.1–3.7 Ga): heavy bombardment, valley networks, lakes (e.g. Jezero, Gale), clay (phyllosilicate) formation — the most habitable surface conditions. Hesperian (~3.7–3.0 Ga): widespread volcanism, outflow channels, sulfate-rich deposits, drying climate. Amazonian (~3.0 Ga–present): cold, dry, low erosion rates; glaciers, polar deposits, recent small-scale volcanism (Cerberus Fossae lavas are geologically young). Carries THEMIS (Thermal Emission Imaging System — the source of NeuroNexus historical thermal evidence) and the Gamma Ray Spectrometer, which detected abundant near-surface hydrogen (water ice) at high latitudes. It is the longest-operating spacecraft at Mars; verify its current status. Mars Express (ESA): orbit 25 December 2003; HRSC stereo camera, OMEGA spectrometer, MARSIS radar. Its Beagle 2 lander (UK) failed to communicate; HiRISE found it partially deployed on the surface in 2015. Spirit (MER-A, NASA): landed 4 January 2004 in Gusev crater; found evidence of hydrothermal activity (silica-rich deposits at Home Plate). Became stuck in 2009; last communication 22 March 2010. Opportunity (MER-B, NASA): landed 25 January 2004 in Meridiani Planum; found hematite "blueberries" and sulfate rocks that formed in acidic water; explored Victoria and Endeavour craters. It drove 45.16 km. That set the off-world driving distance record. Its last contact was 10 June 2018 during the MY 34 global dust storm, and the mission was declared complete on 13 February 2019. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO, NASA): orbit 10 March 2006. Carries HiRISE (~25–30 cm/pixel), CTX (~6 m/pixel), CRISM, SHARAD radar and MCS. It is a key communications relay. Phoenix (NASA): landed 25 May 2008 at ~68° N in Vastitas Borealis; confirmed near-surface water ice an [KNOWLEDGE:mars_missions.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Human exploration: architecture and constraints
excerpt: Transit: Hohmann-like transfers take ~6–9 months each way. Departure windows open every ~26 months. A conjunction-class mission lasts ~2.5–3 years in total with ~500 days on the surface. An opposition-class mission is shorter overall (~1.5–2 years) but has only ~30–60 days on the surface and higher Δv. Entry, descent and landing for human-class payloads (tens of tonnes) is unsolved at scale. Supersonic retropropulsion and inflatable decelerators (e.g. LOFTID) are being matured. Communications delay is 3–22 min one way, and there is a ~2-week blackout at solar conjunction. Crews must operate autonomously; NeuroNexus' deterministic, offline-capable planning tools are designed with this in mind. Radiation: the surface dose is ~0.64 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD). Shielding options are regolith berms, water walls, lava tubes and subsurface habitats; storm shelters are needed for solar particle events. Dust: fine, abrasive and electrostatically charged; contains perchlorates (a thyroid toxin); degrades seals, solar arrays and thermal radiators. Suitports, dust-tolerant mechanisms and airlock cleaning are required. Temperature: night lows below −80 °C are routine at mid-latitudes, so habitats, rovers and suits need active thermal control. Gravity: 0.38 g. Long-term health effects of partial gravity are unknown; crews arrive deconditioned after months in microgravity. # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Global topography and major regions
excerpt: Elevations are referenced to the MOLA areoid (an equipotential surface); the MOLA global topography dataset (Smith et al. 2001) has ~1 m vertical precision and is the basis for NeuroNexus terrain (MEGDR 128 pixels/degree ≈ 463 m/pixel at the equator). Hemispheric dichotomy: rugged, heavily cratered southern highlands vs. smooth, low northern plains (several km lower). Tharsis: a vast volcanic rise (~5,000 km across) hosting Olympus Mons (summit ≈ 21.9 km above the datum, ~600 km wide — the tallest volcano in the solar system) and the three Tharsis Montes (Arsia, Pavonis, Ascraeus Mons). Valles Marineris: canyon system ~4,000 km long, up to ~7 km deep and ~200 km wide. Hellas Planitia: impact basin ~2,300 km across; its floor (≈ −7.2 km) is the lowest broad region on Mars. Other key regions: Argyre and Isidis basins; Elysium volcanic province; Arabia Terra; Utopia, Acidalia, Chryse and Amazonis Planitiae; the north and south polar layered deposits. Named-feature conventions (IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature): crater; mons (mountain); patera (shallow volcano); vallis (valley); chasma (canyon); planitia (low plain); planum (high plain); terra (extensive land mass); fossae (troughs); labyrinthus (intersecting valleys); dorsum (ridge); tholus (small domical mountain). # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Observation history
excerpt: Ancient astronomers tracked Mars' retrograde loops. Its red colour linked it to war gods (Nergal, Ares, Mars). Galileo first observed Mars telescopically in 1610. Christiaan Huygens drew the first surface feature, Syrtis Major, in 1659 and estimated the rotation period. Giovanni Cassini refined the period and noted the polar caps (1666). William Herschel measured the axial tilt and noted seasonal polar cap changes (1780s). 1877 opposition: Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped "canali" (channels), mistranslated as "canals". Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos. Percival Lowell (1890s–1910s) popularised the idea of artificial canals. Better telescopes (Antoniadi, 1909) and later Mariner 4 (1965) showed the canals were optical illusions. Spacecraft era: see the missions reference. Key paradigm shifts: Mariner 4 showed a Moon-like cratered planet. Mariner 9 revealed volcanoes, canyons and ancient channels. Viking searched for life. MGS, Odyssey, MRO and the rovers established a wet, potentially habitable ancient Mars. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Radiation environment
excerpt: Mars lacks a global magnetic field and has a thin atmosphere (~16–20 g/cm² column vs. ~1,000 g/cm² on Earth). Curiosity RAD measured ≈ 0.64 ± 0.12 mSv/day on the surface at Gale (Hassler et al. 2014) and ≈ 1.8 mSv/day during cruise. A ~860-day reference mission (cruise + 500 days on the surface) accumulates roughly 1 Sv in total — comparable to or above career limits under older NASA standards. Solar particle events add acute risk; shielding with regolith, water or subsurface habitats reduces dose. Lower-elevation sites have slightly more atmospheric shielding. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Water and ice
excerpt: Polar caps: north residual cap is mostly water ice (~1,000 km across, layered deposits up to ~3 km thick); the south residual cap has a thin CO₂ ice veneer over water ice. Ground ice is widespread poleward of ~±40–50° latitude; Phoenix (2008, 68° N) exposed water ice a few centimetres below the surface. Fresh impact craters and exposed scarps (HiRISE) reveal relatively pure ice at mid-latitudes, important for human ISRU. Ancient water evidence: valley networks, deltas (Jezero, Eberswalde), lake sediments (Gale), hydrated minerals (clays, sulfates, carbonates), hematite concretions (Meridiani). Recurring slope lineae (RSL) were once proposed as brines but are now widely interpreted as granular flows; treat claims of present-day liquid water with caution. Perchlorate salts (found by Phoenix, confirmed by Curiosity) are common in the soil; they are toxic to humans and lower the freezing point of brines. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: What should the crew know about water and ice?

Polar caps: north residual cap is mostly water ice (~1,000 km across, layered deposits up to ~3 km thick); the south residual cap has a thin CO₂ ice veneer over water ice. # Knowledge base: mars_missions.md / 2012–2020
excerpt: Curiosity / Mars Science Laboratory (NASA): landed 6 August 2012 (UTC) in Gale crater using the Sky Crane. It is a nuclear-powered (MMRTG) rover climbing Aeolis Mons (Mount Sharp). It established that Gale once held a long-lived, habitable freshwater lake (Yellowknife Bay, 2013). It detected complex organic molecules (2018) and seasonal methane variations. Its RAD instrument measured the surface radiation dose. MAVEN (NASA): orbit 21 September 2014; it studies upper-atmosphere loss to space, and showed that solar-wind stripping removed much of the early atmosphere. Verify its current status. Mars Orbiter Mission / Mangalyaan (ISRO, India): orbit 24 September 2014, India's first interplanetary mission, successful on its first attempt. Contact was lost in 2022. ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (ESA): orbit October 2016; studies trace gases (methane upper limits) and mapped hydrogen; also a relay. Its Schiaparelli demonstrator lander crashed on 19 October 2016. InSight (NASA): landed 26 November 2018 in Elysium Planitia. Its SEIS seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and constrained the size of Mars' crust, mantle and liquid core. The mission ended in December 2022 when dust starved its solar arrays. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_missions.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Observation history
excerpt: Ancient astronomers tracked Mars' retrograde loops. Its red colour linked it to war gods (Nergal, Ares, Mars). Galileo first observed Mars telescopically in 1610. Christiaan Huygens drew the first surface feature, Syrtis Major, in 1659 and estimated the rotation period. Giovanni Cassini refined the period and noted the polar caps (1666). William Herschel measured the axial tilt and noted seasonal polar cap changes (1780s). 1877 opposition: Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped "canali" (channels), mistranslated as "canals". Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos. Percival Lowell (1890s–1910s) popularised the idea of artificial canals. Better telescopes (Antoniadi, 1909) and later Mariner 4 (1965) showed the canals were optical illusions. Spacecraft era: see the missions reference. Key paradigm shifts: Mariner 4 showed a Moon-like cratered planet. Mariner 9 revealed volcanoes, canyons and ancient channels. Viking searched for life. MGS, Odyssey, MRO and the rovers established a wet, potentially habitable ancient Mars. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

QUESTION: What should the crew know about observation history?
Ancient astronomers tracked Mars' retrograde loops. Its red color linked it to war gods (Nergal, Ares, Mars). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Selecting a human landing site / exploration zone
excerpt: NASA's First Landing Site/Exploration Zone Workshop (2015) defined an Exploration Zone (EZ) as ~100 km in radius around a landing site. Criteria: Engineering: latitude within ~±50° for solar power and thermal reasons; low elevation (below about +2 km MOLA) so the atmosphere helps braking; low slopes and rock abundance at the landing ellipse; load-bearing surfaces. Resources: accessible water ice or hydrated minerals; potential construction materials. Science: Regions of Interest (ROIs) with diverse, ancient geology (astrobiology, climate, volcanism) within traverse range. Operations: safe traverses for pressurised rovers and EVA. Walkback distance to the habitat drives EVA planning. NeuroNexus shows candidate Potential Exploration Zones in the 3D view. These are planning context, not certified sites. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_missions.md / Overview and success rate
excerpt: Many Mars missions have failed (launch failures, cruise losses, landing failures). # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Seasons and solar longitude (Ls)
excerpt: Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Because of the eccentric orbit, perihelion falls near Ls 251° (southern late spring/summer). Southern summers are shorter and hotter; northern summers longer and cooler. The dusty season is roughly Ls 180°–360° (southern spring/summer); regional storms are common then and planet-encircling (global) dust storms occur in some years. Mars Years (MY) follow the Clancy et al. (2000) convention: MY 1 began on 11 April 1955 (Ls 0). MY 34 began 5 May 2017; MY 35 began 23 March 2019; MY 37 began 26 December 2022; MY 38 began 12 November 2024. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: Quick explainer on seasons and solar longitude (ls)?

Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Because of the eccentric orbit, perihelion falls near Ls 251° (southern late spring/summer). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Global topography and major regions
excerpt: Elevations are referenced to the MOLA areoid (an equipotential surface); the MOLA global topography dataset (Smith et al. 2001) has ~1 m vertical precision and is the basis for NeuroNexus terrain (MEGDR 128 pixels/degree ≈ 463 m/pixel at the equator). Hemispheric dichotomy: rugged, heavily cratered southern highlands vs. smooth, low northern plains (several km lower). Tharsis: a vast volcanic rise (~5,000 km across) hosting Olympus Mons (summit ≈ 21.9 km above the datum, ~600 km wide — the tallest volcano in the solar system) and the three Tharsis Montes (Arsia, Pavonis, Ascraeus Mons). Valles Marineris: canyon system ~4,000 km long, up to ~7 km deep and ~200 km wide. Hellas Planitia: impact basin ~2,300 km across; its floor (≈ −7.2 km) is the lowest broad region on Mars. Other key regions: Argyre and Isidis basins; Elysium volcanic province; Arabia Terra; Utopia, Acidalia, Chryse and Amazonis Planitiae; the north and south polar layered deposits. Named-feature conventions (IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature): crater; mons (mountain); patera (shallow volcano); vallis (valley); chasma (canyon); planitia (low plain); planum (high plain); terra (extensive land mass); fossae (troughs); labyrinthus (intersecting valleys); dorsum (ridge); tholus (small domical mountain). # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Atmosphere
excerpt: Composition (Curiosity SAM, Gale crater): ≈ 95% CO₂, ≈ 2.6–2.8% N₂, ≈ 1.9–2.0% Ar, ≈ 0.16–0.17% O₂, ≈ 0.06% CO, plus trace H₂O and other species. Exact fractions vary seasonally. Mean surface pressure ≈ 600 Pa (≈ 0.6% of Earth's). It varies by ~25–30% over the year as CO₂ freezes onto and sublimes from the seasonal polar caps, and strongly with elevation: ~1,100+ Pa in Hellas, well under 100 Pa at the top of Olympus Mons. 610 Pa is the reference "mean" pressure used to normalise dust optical depths (Montabone et al.). Temperatures: global mean ≈ 210 K (−63 °C). Surface extremes span roughly −125 °C (polar night, CO₂ frost point ≈ 148 K at 600 Pa) to about +20 °C (equatorial summer afternoons, dark surfaces). The thin air holds little heat, so diurnal swings of 70–100 K are normal. Liquid water is unstable at the surface almost everywhere: pressure is near the triple point of water (611.657 Pa). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Selecting a human landing site / exploration zone
excerpt: NASA's First Landing Site/Exploration Zone Workshop (2015) defined an Exploration Zone (EZ) as ~100 km in radius around a landing site. Criteria: Engineering: latitude within ~±50° for solar power and thermal reasons; low elevation (below about +2 km MOLA) so the atmosphere helps braking; low slopes and rock abundance at the landing ellipse; load-bearing surfaces. Resources: accessible water ice or hydrated minerals; potential construction materials. Science: Regions of Interest (ROIs) with diverse, ancient geology (astrobiology, climate, volcanism) within traverse range. Operations: safe traverses for pressurised rovers and EVA. Walkback distance to the habitat drives EVA planning. NeuroNexus shows candidate Potential Exploration Zones in the 3D view. These are planning context, not certified sites. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Observation history
excerpt: Ancient astronomers tracked Mars' retrograde loops. Its red colour linked it to war gods (Nergal, Ares, Mars). Galileo first observed Mars telescopically in 1610. Christiaan Huygens drew the first surface feature, Syrtis Major, in 1659 and estimated the rotation period. Giovanni Cassini refined the period and noted the polar caps (1666). William Herschel measured the axial tilt and noted seasonal polar cap changes (1780s). 1877 opposition: Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped "canali" (channels), mistranslated as "canals". Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos. Percival Lowell (1890s–1910s) popularised the idea of artificial canals. Better telescopes (Antoniadi, 1909) and later Mariner 4 (1965) showed the canals were optical illusions. Spacecraft era: see the missions reference. Key paradigm shifts: Mariner 4 showed a Moon-like cratered planet. Mariner 9 revealed volcanoes, canyons and ancient channels. Viking searched for life. MGS, Odyssey, MRO and the rovers established a wet, potentially habitable ancient Mars. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Seasons and solar longitude (Ls)
excerpt: Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Because of the eccentric orbit, perihelion falls near Ls 251° (southern late spring/summer). Southern summers are shorter and hotter; northern summers longer and cooler. The dusty season is roughly Ls 180°–360° (southern spring/summer); regional storms are common then and planet-encircling (global) dust storms occur in some years. Mars Years (MY) follow the Clancy et al. (2000) convention: MY 1 began on 11 April 1955 (Ls 0). MY 34 began 5 May 2017; MY 35 began 23 March 2019; MY 37 began 26 December 2022; MY 38 began 12 November 2024. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. excerpt: Mars lacks a global magnetic field and has a thin atmosphere (~16–20 g/cm² column vs. ~1,000 g/cm² on Earth). # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Seasons and solar longitude (Ls)
excerpt: Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Because of the eccentric orbit, perihelion falls near Ls 251° (southern late spring/summer). Southern summers are shorter and hotter; northern summers longer and cooler. The dusty season is roughly Ls 180°–360° (southern spring/summer); regional storms are common then and planet-encircling (global) dust storms occur in some years. Mars Years (MY) follow the Clancy et al. (2000) convention: MY 1 began on 11 April 1955 (Ls 0). MY 34 began 5 May 2017; MY 35 began 23 March 2019; MY 37 began 26 December 2022; MY 38 began 12 November 2024. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Noachian (~4.1–3.7 Ga): heavy bombardment, valley networks, lakes (e.g. Jezero, Gale), clay (phyllosilicate) formation — the most habitable surface conditions. Hesperian (~3.7–3.0 Ga): widespread volcanism, outflow channels, sulfate-rich deposits, drying climate. Amazonian (~3.0 Ga–present): cold, dry, low erosion rates; glaciers, polar deposits, recent small-scale volcanism (Cerberus Fossae lavas are geologically young). Boundary ages are approximate (crater-count model ages). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

excerpt: 2001 Mars Odyssey (NASA): orbit 24 October 2001. Carries THEMIS (Thermal Emission Imaging System — the source of NeuroNexus historical thermal evidence) and the Gamma Ray Spectrometer, which detected abundant near-surface hydrogen (water ice) at high latitudes. It is the longest-operating spacecraft at Mars; verify its current status. Mars Express (ESA): orbit 25 December 2003; HRSC stereo camera, OMEGA spectrometer, MARSIS radar. Its Beagle 2 lander (UK) failed to communicate; HiRISE found it partially deployed on the surface in 2015. Spirit (MER-A, NASA): landed 4 January 2004 in Gusev crater; found evidence of hydrothermal activity (silica-rich deposits at Home Plate). Became stuck in 2009; last communication 22 March 2010. Opportunity (MER-B, NASA): landed 25 January 2004 in Meridiani Planum; found hematite "blueberries" and sulfate rocks that formed in acidic water; explored Victoria and Endeavour craters. It drove 45.16 km. That set the off-world driving distance record. Its last contact was 10 June 2018 during the MY 34 global dust storm, and the mission was declared complete on 13 February 2019. Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO, NASA): orbit 10 March 2006. Carries HiRISE (~25–30 cm/pixel), CTX (~6 m/pixel), CRISM, SHARAD radar and MCS. It is a key communications relay. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Observation history
excerpt: Ancient astronomers tracked Mars' retrograde loops. Its red colour linked it to war gods (Nergal, Ares, Mars). Galileo first observed Mars telescopically in 1610. Christiaan Huygens drew the first surface feature, Syrtis Major, in 1659 and estimated the rotation period. Giovanni Cassini refined the period and noted the polar caps (1666). William Herschel measured the axial tilt and noted seasonal polar cap changes (1780s). 1877 opposition: Giovanni Schiaparelli mapped "canali" (channels), mistranslated as "canals". Asaph Hall discovered Phobos and Deimos. Percival Lowell (1890s–1910s) popularised the idea of artificial canals. Better telescopes (Antoniadi, 1909) and later Mariner 4 (1965) showed the canals were optical illusions. Spacecraft era: see the missions reference. Key paradigm shifts: Mariner 4 showed a Moon-like cratered planet. Mariner 9 revealed volcanoes, canyons and ancient channels. Viking searched for life. MGS, Odyssey, MRO and the rovers established a wet, potentially habitable ancient Mars. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Water and ice
excerpt: Polar caps: north residual cap is mostly water ice (~1,000 km across, layered deposits up to ~3 km thick); the south residual cap has a thin CO₂ ice veneer over water ice. Ground ice is widespread poleward of ~±40–50° latitude; Phoenix (2008, 68° N) exposed water ice a few centimetres below the surface. Fresh impact craters and exposed scarps (HiRISE) reveal relatively pure ice at mid-latitudes, important for human ISRU. Ancient water evidence: valley networks, deltas (Jezero, Eberswalde), lake sediments (Gale), hydrated minerals (clays, sulfates, carbonates), hematite concretions (Meridiani). Recurring slope lineae (RSL) were once proposed as brines but are now widely interpreted as granular flows; treat claims of present-day liquid water with caution. Perchlorate salts (found by Phoenix, confirmed by Curiosity) are common in the soil; they are toxic to humans and lower the freezing point of brines. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Global topography and major regions
excerpt: Elevations are referenced to the MOLA areoid (an equipotential surface); the MOLA global topography dataset (Smith et al. 2001) has ~1 m vertical precision and is the basis for NeuroNexus terrain (MEGDR 128 pixels/degree ≈ 463 m/pixel at the equator). Hemispheric dichotomy: rugged, heavily cratered southern highlands vs. smooth, low northern plains (several km lower). Tharsis: a vast volcanic rise (~5,000 km across) hosting Olympus Mons (summit ≈ 21.9 km above the datum, ~600 km wide — the tallest volcano in the solar system) and the three Tharsis Montes (Arsia, Pavonis, Ascraeus Mons). Valles Marineris: canyon system ~4,000 km long, up to ~7 km deep and ~200 km wide. Hellas Planitia: impact basin ~2,300 km across; its floor (≈ −7.2 km) is the lowest broad region on Mars. Other key regions: Argyre and Isidis basins; Elysium volcanic province; Arabia Terra; Utopia, Acidalia, Chryse and Amazonis Planitiae; the north and south polar layered deposits. Named-feature conventions (IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature): crater; mons (mountain); patera (shallow volcano); vallis (valley); chasma (canyon); planitia (low plain); planum (high plain); terra (extensive land mass); fossae (troughs); labyrinthus (intersecting valleys); dorsum (ridge); tholus (small domical mountain). # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Mars time keeping
excerpt: A sol is 24 h 39 m 35 s. Mission teams count sols from landing (Curiosity sol 0 = 6 August 2012). Local Mean Solar Time (LMST) and Local True Solar Time (LTST) are used for operations. "Mars time" shifts ~40 minutes later each Earth day, which is hard on ground crews. Coordinated Mars Time (MTC) is the mean solar time at the prime meridian (Airy-0 crater). Longitude conventions: modern NASA and USGS products use planetocentric latitude and east-positive longitude 0–360° (NeuroNexus uses this). Older maps used planetographic latitude and west longitude. Mission awareness: Crewed Mars console (mission profile, EVA, life support, resources), NASA/JPL near-Mars small-body close-approach tracking, and the NASA Mars reference feed. Mars Intelligence: a Gemini-powered assistant that answers from application tools, a curated Mars knowledge base and project documentation, with optional Google Search grounding. excerpt: EVA time is estimated from distance divided by pace, plus an ascent allowance (metres climbed per hour). In NeuroNexus the defaults are 2.5 km/h and 600 m/h, and both are user adjustable. Safe Haven: in NeuroNexus, a user-designated retreat point (habitat, cache, rover). Routes report the maximum distance from the nearest Safe Haven. excerpt: Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Because of the eccentric orbit, perihelion falls near Ls 251° (southern late spring/summer). Southern summers are shorter and hotter; northern summers longer and cooler. The dusty season is roughly Ls 180°–360° (southern spring/summer); regional storms are common then and planet-encircling (global) dust storms occur in some years. Mars Years (MY) follow the Clancy et al. (2000) convention: MY 1 began on 11 April 1955 (Ls 0). MY 34 began 5 May 2017; MY 35 began 23 March 2019; MY 37 began 26 December 2022; MY 38 began 12 November 2024. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Selecting a human landing site / exploration zone
excerpt: NASA's First Landing Site/Exploration Zone Workshop (2015) defined an Exploration Zone (EZ) as ~100 km in radius around a landing site. Criteria: Engineering: latitude within ~±50° for solar power and thermal reasons; low elevation (below about +2 km MOLA) so the atmosphere helps braking; low slopes and rock abundance at the landing ellipse; load-bearing surfaces. Resources: accessible water ice or hydrated minerals; potential construction materials. Science: Regions of Interest (ROIs) with diverse, ancient geology (astrobiology, climate, volcanism) within traverse range. Operations: safe traverses for pressurised rovers and EVA. Walkback distance to the habitat drives EVA planning. NeuroNexus shows candidate Potential Exploration Zones in the 3D view. These are planning context, not certified sites. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

QUESTION: Quick explainer on selecting a human landing site / exploration zone?

NASA's First Landing Site/Exploration Zone Workshop (2015) defined an Exploration Zone (EZ) as ~100 km in radius around a landing site. Criteria: Engineering: latitude within ~±50° for solar power and thermal reasons; low elevation (below about +2 km MOLA) so the atmosphere helps braking; low slopes and rock abundance at the landing ellipse; load-bearing surfaces. # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Water and ice
excerpt: Polar caps: north residual cap is mostly water ice (~1,000 km across, layered deposits up to ~3 km thick); the south residual cap has a thin CO₂ ice veneer over water ice. Ground ice is widespread poleward of ~±40–50° latitude; Phoenix (2008, 68° N) exposed water ice a few centimetres below the surface. Fresh impact craters and exposed scarps (HiRISE) reveal relatively pure ice at mid-latitudes, important for human ISRU. Ancient water evidence: valley networks, deltas (Jezero, Eberswalde), lake sediments (Gale), hydrated minerals (clays, sulfates, carbonates), hematite concretions (Meridiani). Recurring slope lineae (RSL) were once proposed as brines but are now widely interpreted as granular flows; treat claims of present-day liquid water with caution. Perchlorate salts (found by Phoenix, confirmed by Curiosity) are common in the soil; they are toxic to humans and lower the freezing point of brines. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Dust, dust storms and dust devils
excerpt: Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. Planet-encircling dust storms occurred in 1971 (Mariner 9 arrival), 1977 (two, Viking era), 2001, 2007 and 2018 (MY 34). The 2018 storm began near Ls ≈ 185° and ended the Opportunity rover's mission (power loss, last contact 10 June 2018). Dust lowers daytime surface temperature, raises atmospheric temperature, cuts solar-array output and increases electrostatic and abrasion hazards for hardware and EVA suits. Dust devils are common in spring and summer; they cleaned Spirit's and Opportunity's solar arrays several times. The Montabone et al. (2015) climatology reconstructs daily gridded column dust optical depth for MY 24 onward from orbiter (TES, THEMIS, MCS) retrievals. The NASA Ames Mars GCM V3.2 distributes it as DustScenario_MYxx.nc files (3° × 3° bins, daily) — this is the source of the NeuroNexus dust panel (variable `tau`, with `zmax` the dust-top altitude in km of the modified Conrath vertical profile). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: Quick explainer on dust, dust storms and dust devils?

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Global topography and major regions
excerpt: Elevations are referenced to the MOLA areoid (an equipotential surface); the MOLA global topography dataset (Smith et al. 2001) has ~1 m vertical precision and is the basis for NeuroNexus terrain (MEGDR 128 pixels/degree ≈ 463 m/pixel at the equator). Hemispheric dichotomy: rugged, heavily cratered southern highlands vs. smooth, low northern plains (several km lower). Tharsis: a vast volcanic rise (~5,000 km across) hosting Olympus Mons (summit ≈ 21.9 km above the datum, ~600 km wide — the tallest volcano in the solar system) and the three Tharsis Montes (Arsia, Pavonis, Ascraeus Mons). Valles Marineris: canyon system ~4,000 km long, up to ~7 km deep and ~200 km wide. Hellas Planitia: impact basin ~2,300 km across; its floor (≈ −7.2 km) is the lowest broad region on Mars. Other key regions: Argyre and Isidis basins; Elysium volcanic province; Arabia Terra; Utopia, Acidalia, Chryse and Amazonis Planitiae; the north and south polar layered deposits. Named-feature conventions (IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature): crater; mons (mountain); patera (shallow volcano); vallis (valley); chasma (canyon); planitia (low plain); planum (high plain); terra (extensive land mass); fossae (troughs); labyrinthus (intersecting valleys); dorsum (ridge); tholus (small domical mountain). # Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Atmosphere
excerpt: Composition (Curiosity SAM, Gale crater): ≈ 95% CO₂, ≈ 2.6–2.8% N₂, ≈ 1.9–2.0% Ar, ≈ 0.16–0.17% O₂, ≈ 0.06% CO, plus trace H₂O and other species. Exact fractions vary seasonally. Mean surface pressure ≈ 600 Pa (≈ 0.6% of Earth's). It varies by ~25–30% over the year as CO₂ freezes onto and sublimes from the seasonal polar caps, and strongly with elevation: ~1,100+ Pa in Hellas, well under 100 Pa at the top of Olympus Mons. 610 Pa is the reference "mean" pressure used to normalise dust optical depths (Montabone et al.). Temperatures: global mean ≈ 210 K (−63 °C). Surface extremes span roughly −125 °C (polar night, CO₂ frost point ≈ 148 K at 600 Pa) to about +20 °C (equatorial summer afternoons, dark surfaces). The thin air holds little heat, so diurnal swings of 70–100 K are normal. Liquid water is unstable at the surface almost everywhere: pressure is near the triple point of water (611.657 Pa). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / In-situ resource utilisation (ISRU)
excerpt: Oxygen from atmospheric CO₂ by solid-oxide electrolysis. Perseverance MOXIE produced 122 g O₂ in total, up to ~12 g/h at ~98% purity. Water from ground ice (mid and high latitudes) or hydrated minerals. Water is the key resource for life support, radiation shielding and propellant. Methane/oxygen propellant via the Sabatier reaction (CO₂ + H₂ → CH₄ + H₂O), the basis of many return-vehicle concepts. Regolith for shielding, construction (sintering, 3D printing) and agriculture after perchlorate removal. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Seasons and solar longitude (Ls)
excerpt: Seasons are tracked by areocentric solar longitude Ls: Ls 0° = northern spring equinox, 90° = northern summer solstice, 180° = northern autumn equinox, 270° = northern winter solstice. Because of the eccentric orbit, perihelion falls near Ls 251° (southern late spring/summer). Southern summers are shorter and hotter; northern summers longer and cooler. The dusty season is roughly Ls 180°–360° (southern spring/summer); regional storms are common then and planet-encircling (global) dust storms occur in some years. Mars Years (MY) follow the Clancy et al. (2000) convention: MY 1 began on 11 April 1955 (Ls 0). MY 34 began 5 May 2017; MY 35 began 23 March 2019; MY 37 began 26 December 2022; MY 38 began 12 November 2024. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Human exploration: architecture and constraints
excerpt: Transit: Hohmann-like transfers take ~6–9 months each way. Departure windows open every ~26 months. A conjunction-class mission lasts ~2.5–3 years in total with ~500 days on the surface. An opposition-class mission is shorter overall (~1.5–2 years) but has only ~30–60 days on the surface and higher Δv. Entry, descent and landing for human-class payloads (tens of tonnes) is unsolved at scale. Supersonic retropropulsion and inflatable decelerators (e.g. LOFTID) are being matured. Communications delay is 3–22 min one way, and there is a ~2-week blackout at solar conjunction. Crews must operate autonomously; NeuroNexus' deterministic, offline-capable planning tools are designed with this in mind. Radiation: the surface dose is ~0.64 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD). Shielding options are regolith berms, water walls, lava tubes and subsurface habitats; storm shelters are needed for solar particle events. Dust: fine, abrasive and electrostatically charged; contains perchlorates (a thyroid toxin); degrades seals, solar arrays and thermal radiators. Suitports, dust-tolerant mechanisms and airlock cleaning are required. Temperature: night lows below −80 °C are routine at mid-latitudes, so habitats, rovers and suits need active thermal control. Gravity: 0.38 g. Long-term health effects of partial gravity are unknown; crews arrive deconditioned after months in microgravity. # Knowledge base: mars_missions.md / 2012–2020
excerpt: Curiosity / Mars Science Laboratory (NASA): landed 6 August 2012 (UTC) in Gale crater using the Sky Crane. It is a nuclear-powered (MMRTG) rover climbing Aeolis Mons (Mount Sharp). It established that Gale once held a long-lived, habitable freshwater lake (Yellowknife Bay, 2013). It detected complex organic molecules (2018) and seasonal methane variations. Its RAD instrument measured the surface radiation dose. MAVEN (NASA): orbit 21 September 2014; it studies upper-atmosphere loss to space, and showed that solar-wind stripping removed much of the early atmosphere. Verify its current status. Mars Orbiter Mission / Mangalyaan (ISRO, India): orbit 24 September 2014, India's first interplanetary mission, successful on its first attempt. Contact was lost in 2022. ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (ESA): orbit October 2016; studies trace gases (methane upper limits) and mapped hydrogen; also a relay. Its Schiaparelli demonstrator lander crashed on 19 October 2016. InSight (NASA): landed 26 November 2018 in Elysium Planitia. Its SEIS seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and constrained the size of Mars' crust, mantle and liquid core. The mission ended in December 2022 when dust starved its solar arrays. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_missions.md]

CONTEXT:
# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Dust, dust storms and dust devils
excerpt: Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. Planet-encircling dust storms occurred in 1971 (Mariner 9 arrival), 1977 (two, Viking era), 2001, 2007 and 2018 (MY 34). The 2018 storm began near Ls ≈ 185° and ended the Opportunity rover's mission (power loss, last contact 10 June 2018). Dust lowers daytime surface temperature, raises atmospheric temperature, cuts solar-array output and increases electrostatic and abrasion hazards for hardware and EVA suits. Dust devils are common in spring and summer; they cleaned Spirit's and Opportunity's solar arrays several times. The Montabone et al. (2015) climatology reconstructs daily gridded column dust optical depth for MY 24 onward from orbiter (TES, THEMIS, MCS) retrievals. The NASA Ames Mars GCM V3.2 distributes it as DustScenario_MYxx.nc files (3° × 3° bins, daily) — this is the source of the NeuroNexus dust panel (variable `tau`, with `zmax` the dust-top altitude in km of the modified Conrath vertical profile). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: What should the crew know about dust, dust storms and dust devils?

Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / EVA and traverse planning concepts used in NeuroNexus
excerpt: EVA time is estimated from distance divided by pace, plus an ascent allowance (metres climbed per hour). In NeuroNexus the defaults are 2.5 km/h and 600 m/h, and both are user adjustable. Slope: Apollo-era and analog studies suggest walking becomes markedly harder above ~15° and rovers are commonly limited to ~15–30° depending on design. Roughness: here this means local elevation variability (m) in a 3×3 MOLA neighbourhood, a coarse (~460 m pixel) proxy. It does not resolve boulders; HiRISE-scale data is needed for that. Safe Haven: in NeuroNexus, a user-designated retreat point (habitat, cache, rover). Routes report the maximum distance from the nearest Safe Haven. This is a planning aid only; nothing in NeuroNexus certifies a location as safe. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

excerpt: A sol is 24 h 39 m 35 s. Mission teams count sols from landing (Curiosity sol 0 = 6 August 2012). Local Mean Solar Time (LMST) and Local True Solar Time (LTST) are used for operations. Longitude conventions: modern NASA and USGS products use planetocentric latitude and east-positive longitude 0–360° (NeuroNexus uses this). Older maps used planetographic latitude and west longitude. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Human exploration: architecture and constraints
excerpt: Transit: Hohmann-like transfers take ~6–9 months each way. Departure windows open every ~26 months. A conjunction-class mission lasts ~2.5–3 years in total with ~500 days on the surface. An opposition-class mission is shorter overall (~1.5–2 years) but has only ~30–60 days on the surface and higher Δv. Entry, descent and landing for human-class payloads (tens of tonnes) is unsolved at scale. Supersonic retropropulsion and inflatable decelerators (e.g. LOFTID) are being matured. Communications delay is 3–22 min one way, and there is a ~2-week blackout at solar conjunction. Crews must operate autonomously; NeuroNexus' deterministic, offline-capable planning tools are designed with this in mind. Radiation: the surface dose is ~0.64 mSv/day (Curiosity RAD). Shielding options are regolith berms, water walls, lava tubes and subsurface habitats; storm shelters are needed for solar particle events. Dust: fine, abrasive and electrostatically charged; contains perchlorates (a thyroid toxin); degrades seals, solar arrays and thermal radiators. Suitports, dust-tolerant mechanisms and airlock cleaning are required. Temperature: night lows below −80 °C are routine at mid-latitudes, so habitats, rovers and suits need active thermal control. Gravity: 0.38 g. Long-term health effects of partial gravity are unknown; crews arrive deconditioned after months in microgravity. # Knowledge base: mars_history_and_human_exploration.md / Selecting a human landing site / exploration zone
excerpt: NASA's First Landing Site/Exploration Zone Workshop (2015) defined an Exploration Zone (EZ) as ~100 km in radius around a landing site. Criteria: Engineering: latitude within ~±50° for solar power and thermal reasons; low elevation (below about +2 km MOLA) so the atmosphere helps braking; low slopes and rock abundance at the landing ellipse; load-bearing surfaces. Resources: accessible water ice or hydrated minerals; potential construction materials. Science: Regions of Interest (ROIs) with diverse, ancient geology (astrobiology, climate, volcanism) within traverse range. Operations: safe traverses for pressurised rovers and EVA. Walkback distance to the habitat drives EVA planning. NeuroNexus shows candidate Potential Exploration Zones in the 3D view. These are planning context, not certified sites. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

QUESTION: What should the crew know about selecting a human landing site / exploration zone?

NASA's First Landing Site/Exploration Zone Workshop (2015) defined an Exploration Zone (EZ) as ~100 km in radius around a landing site. Criteria: Engineering: latitude within ~±50° for solar power and thermal reasons; low elevation (below about +2 km MOLA) so the atmosphere helps braking; low slopes and rock abundance at the landing ellipse; load-bearing surfaces. Resources: accessible water ice or hydrated minerals; potential construction materials. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_history_and_human_exploration.md]

excerpt: Curiosity / Mars Science Laboratory (NASA): landed 6 August 2012 (UTC) in Gale crater using the Sky Crane. It is a nuclear-powered (MMRTG) rover climbing Aeolis Mons (Mount Sharp). It established that Gale once held a long-lived, habitable freshwater lake (Yellowknife Bay, 2013). It detected complex organic molecules (2018) and seasonal methane variations. Its RAD instrument measured the surface radiation dose. MAVEN (NASA): orbit 21 September 2014; it studies upper-atmosphere loss to space, and showed that solar-wind stripping removed much of the early atmosphere. Verify its current status. Mars Orbiter Mission / Mangalyaan (ISRO, India): orbit 24 September 2014, India's first interplanetary mission, successful on its first attempt. Contact was lost in 2022. ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (ESA): orbit October 2016; studies trace gases (methane upper limits) and mapped hydrogen; also a relay. Its Schiaparelli demonstrator lander crashed on 19 October 2016. InSight (NASA): landed 26 November 2018 in Elysium Planitia. Its SEIS seismometer recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes and constrained the size of Mars' crust, mantle and liquid core. The mission ended in December 2022 when dust starved its solar arrays. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_missions.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Dust, dust storms and dust devils
excerpt: Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. Planet-encircling dust storms occurred in 1971 (Mariner 9 arrival), 1977 (two, Viking era), 2001, 2007 and 2018 (MY 34). The 2018 storm began near Ls ≈ 185° and ended the Opportunity rover's mission (power loss, last contact 10 June 2018). Dust lowers daytime surface temperature, raises atmospheric temperature, cuts solar-array output and increases electrostatic and abrasion hazards for hardware and EVA suits. Dust devils are common in spring and summer; they cleaned Spirit's and Opportunity's solar arrays several times. The Montabone et al. (2015) climatology reconstructs daily gridded column dust optical depth for MY 24 onward from orbiter (TES, THEMIS, MCS) retrievals. The NASA Ames Mars GCM V3.2 distributes it as DustScenario_MYxx.nc files (3° × 3° bins, daily) — this is the source of the NeuroNexus dust panel (variable `tau`, with `zmax` the dust-top altitude in km of the modified Conrath vertical profile). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

QUESTION: Tell me about dust, dust storms and dust devils.

Dust is the dominant short-term weather driver. Column dust optical depth (τ) is the standard measure: τ ≈ 0.2–0.5 is typical background; regional storms push τ above 1; global storms reach τ ≈ 5–10+ in visible wavelengths. [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]

# Knowledge base: mars_planet.md / Global topography and major regions
excerpt: Elevations are referenced to the MOLA areoid (an equipotential surface); the MOLA global topography dataset (Smith et al. 2001) has ~1 m vertical precision and is the basis for NeuroNexus terrain (MEGDR 128 pixels/degree ≈ 463 m/pixel at the equator). Hemispheric dichotomy: rugged, heavily cratered southern highlands vs. smooth, low northern plains (several km lower). Tharsis: a vast volcanic rise (~5,000 km across) hosting Olympus Mons (summit ≈ 21.9 km above the datum, ~600 km wide — the tallest volcano in the solar system) and the three Tharsis Montes (Arsia, Pavonis, Ascraeus Mons). Valles Marineris: canyon system ~4,000 km long, up to ~7 km deep and ~200 km wide. Hellas Planitia: impact basin ~2,300 km across; its floor (≈ −7.2 km) is the lowest broad region on Mars. Other key regions: Argyre and Isidis basins; Elysium volcanic province; Arabia Terra; Utopia, Acidalia, Chryse and Amazonis Planitiae; the north and south polar layered deposits. Named-feature conventions (IAU/USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature): crater; mons (mountain); patera (shallow volcano); vallis (valley); chasma (canyon); planitia (low plain); planum (high plain); terra (extensive land mass); fossae (troughs); labyrinthus (intersecting valleys); dorsum (ridge); tholus (small domical mountain). [KNOWLEDGE:mars_planet.md]
